prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage.
Do not give IV thrombolysis while blood pressure is above 185/110 mmHg.
Do not withhold thrombolysis because he takes aspirin and clopidogrel; antiplatelet therapy is not a contraindication.
Do not give IV thrombolysis if INR is above 1.7, the platelet count is below 100,000, or another guideline contraindication is present.
Do not delay non-contrast CT imaging for additional labs or evaluation in a stroke alert.
Do not delay thrombectomy to observe the response to IV thrombolysis.
Do not treat the mildly raised troponin as a primary acute coronary syndrome without serial troponin and ECG review; neurogenic troponin elevation is common in acute stroke.
Do not leave him off antiplatelet therapy beyond the 24 hours after thrombolysis once imaging excludes haemorrhage: symptomatic intracranial stenosis carries a high early recurrence risk.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (14:20, 38 minutes before arrival) and the NIHSS (12).

IV thrombolysis: give once blood pressure is below 185/110 mmHg (38 minutes from last known well, no haemorrhage on CT, glucose 168 mg/dL, INR 1.0, platelets 242; aspirin and clopidogrel are not contraindications). Thrombectomy: proceed for the right M1 near-occlusion (NIHSS 12, pre-stroke mRS 0, ASPECTS 9, within 6 hours); do not wait for the response to thrombolysis.
Lower blood pressure (188/104 mmHg) below 185/110 mmHg with IV labetalol or nicardipine before IV thrombolysis, then keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours.
Give alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg) or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) with a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes.

Proceed to mechanical thrombectomy for the right M1 near-occlusion, telling the interventional team that CTA shows underlying intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis at the occlusion site; keep blood pressure at or below 185/110 mmHg before the procedure and do not target systolic below 140 mmHg after successful recanalization.
Watch for orolingual angioedema during and after alteplase because he takes lisinopril.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.

Repeat troponin and review the ECG; the mild elevation (0.08 ng/mL) is most likely neurogenic myocardial injury or demand ischaemia on his known three-vessel coronary disease; it does not delay reperfusion.

Give no antiplatelet in the 24 hours after thrombolysis; once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhage, resume aspirin 81 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily for 90 days for the symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis, then review long-term antiplatelet therapy with cardiology for his coronary disease, and address the missed doses.
Intensify lipid lowering (LDL 142 mg/dL on atorvastatin 40 mg): atorvastatin 80 mg, adding ezetimibe if LDL stays at or above 70 mg/dL.
After the acute phase, lower blood pressure to below 130/80 mmHg, improve diabetes control (HbA1c 8.1 percent), and support smoking cessation with counselling and pharmacotherapy (one pack per day).

Intracranial atherosclerotic disease is among the commonest causes of ischaemic stroke worldwide and is more frequent in Asian, Black, Hispanic and Middle Eastern populations with a heavy vascular risk factor burden.

Mild troponin elevation in acute ischaemic stroke often reflects neurogenic myocardial injury from the catecholamine surge or demand ischaemia; serial troponin and ECG review, not reperfusion delay, separate it from a primary coronary syndrome.

TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery atherosclerosis) requires >50% stenosis or occlusion of a major brain artery with a compatible syndrome; ICAD on CTA with eccentric calcification at the occlusion satisfies this.
Symptomatic intracranial stenosis: aspirin plus clopidogrel for 90 days with intensive risk factor control is superior to stenting (SAMMPRIS).
The old right basal ganglia lacune on MRI is a previous silent infarct, so this event is a recurrence in a patient with known small vessel disease.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward — acute onset left hemiplegia + rightward gaze deviation in a 63-year-old Arab male with heavy vascular risk burden; right MCA M1 near-complete occlusion on CTA with underlying ICAD changes; mildly elevated troponin serves as a realistic red herring (neurogenic) but does not obscure the primary diagnosis.

metadata.real_seed_note: Extensive PMC literature search conducted (searched for right MCA LAA male CC-BY case reports); no qualifying CC-BY PMC case report with confirmed right MCA large-artery atherosclerosis in an Arab male patient was identified. Demographics, mechanism, territory, and tool outputs reflect published epidemiology of ICAD in Arab/Middle Eastern populations.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Khalid Al-Rashidi is a 63-year-old right-handed Arab man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, active tobacco use, and known three-vessel coronary artery disease (managed medically, last angiogram 4 years ago) who was brought to the emergency department by his wife after sudden-onset left-sided weakness. The patient and his wife report that he was watching television at home at 14:20 when he suddenly dropped his cup of tea with his left hand and was unable to raise his left arm. He then tried to stand and found his left leg would not support his weight. His wife, who was present throughout, confirms he had no symptoms before this moment. She called emergency services immediately. EMS arrived at 14:35, documented left hemiplegia, left facial droop, and rightward gaze deviation. Field glucose was 168 mg/dL. A prehospital stroke alert was activated and the patient arrived in the ED at 14:58. The patient denies headache, loss of consciousness, preceding visual changes, chest pain, palpitations, nausea, vomiting, or seizure activity. He has no prior history of stroke or TIA. He endorses increased tobacco use over the past year (approximately one pack per day) and acknowledges his blood pressure has not been well-controlled despite two antihypertensive agents — he has not seen his primary care physician in 14 months. He also admits to missing several doses of his aspirin and clopidogrel over the past two weeks because of a gastrointestinal upset. His wife confirms no new medications, herbal supplements, or illicit substances. Time of last known well is established at 14:20, approximately 38 minutes before ED arrival. He speaks primarily Arabic; his son, who arrived shortly after EMS, is assisting with interpretation.
